title: Three Ways to Say Stop
author: Nadina D. Lisbon
summary: Nadina D. Lisbon takes a week of agent-safety announcements and reframes them as a question of leadership. Her central argument is that "stop" is really three different verbs: halt the agent now, keep it from relaunching, or revoke its access. Each answers a different worry and leaves work in a different state. She draws on CrowdStrike's kill switch, OpenAI's Control Room delay, and two surveys showing most organizations cannot yet halt or revoke an agent. The move she makes is to shift attention from the switch to the people downstream of the pause, namely the customer waiting and the analyst with half-built work. The leader's task, on her account, is to know which verb to use and to have calm answers about who is told, who carries the work, and how trust is restored. A short exercise, drafting an unsent Pause Notice, lets readers find the gaps in their own plans.
points: Argues that stopping an AI agent is three distinct acts: halting current work, preventing relaunch, and revoking access.
Uses CrowdStrike's AI Kill Switch and OpenAI's 35-second Control Room delay as evidence that stopping is a process, not a button.
Cites survey figures showing only 17.5% of organizations can automatically stop a misbehaving agent and 26.4% can revoke its access.
Locates the leader's real work in the messages and handoffs around a pause rather than in owning the switch.
Offers a five-minute exercise of drafting an unsent Pause Notice to expose the missing parts of a plan.
quotes: In practice, “stop” covers three very different moves. You can halt what the agent is doing right now. You can keep it from starting again. Or you can take back the access it was given.
Control isn’t a dramatic rescue at the worst possible moment. It’s a steady state, the kind that lets a team give an agent more room because everyone knows the pause is close at hand.

A pause is a process with a beginning, a middle, and an end, and the middle is where the people are: the customer waiting on a reply, the analyst whose report was half-built, the colleague who assumed the agent had it covered.
That’s why the leader’s most valuable role may not be owning the switch at all. It’s knowing which verb you’d reach for in a given moment, and having calm answers to the questions that follow.
When the stop, the restart, and the message to the humans involved have all been thought through, a pause stops feeling like an emergency and starts feeling like ordinary, well-run operations.
A pause control tells you how to stop an agent. It rarely tells you who will notice, or what they’ll be waiting on.
The sentence that was hardest to write usually points to the part of the plan that doesn't exist yet.
